vignette:
Clinical Vignette: Patient A. (30, Female, African, Married, School Counselor)

Over the course of several sessions, A. has slowly begun to share the story she has carried alone for nearly two years. She speaks in fragments, often stopping to stare at the floor, as if she is watching the events unfold again behind her eyes.

The trauma happened on a Tuesday evening in late spring. A. was driving home from a parent-teacher conference, still thinking about a struggling student she had urged to try harder. She was alone, and it was dark. She noticed police lights in her rearview mirror-she had no idea why. She pulled over, heart already pounding, hands gripping the wheel. The officer took too long to approach. When he did, he shouted. He asked where she was going, why she was in that neighborhood, whether she lived there. She tried to explain: I'm a school counselor. I was at work. I'm going home. He told her to step out of the car. She felt the cold metal of the car door against her back. Another officer arrived. They searched her car without her permission. They kept her on the side of the road for forty-five minutes. She did not get a ticket, only a verbal warning and a look that made her feel less than human.

In the weeks following, A. could not stop replaying the moment the first officer put his hand on his holster. She started avoiding driving after dark. Then she stopped driving past that intersection entirely, taking a fifteen-minute detour every day. Her husband, Kofi, noticed she was quieter, more irritable. She told him it was work stress. She did not mention the police.

As a school counselor, A. spends her days helping children navigate anxiety, grief, and fear. She runs small groups on emotional regulation, and she is the one teachers call when a student has a meltdown. She is good at her job. But now, when she hears a knock on her office door, her heart jumps. One morning, a police officer came to the school to give a presentation on safety. A. hid in the bathroom for the entire hour, hands shaking, breathing shallow. Her supervisor later asked if she was sick. She said she had a migraine.

At home, A. has become hypervigilant. She checks the locks three times before bed. She cannot sit with her back to a window in a restaurant. She startles when Kofi walks into a room too quietly. He has asked, gently, why she flinches when he touches her shoulder from behind. She says she is just tired. But she is not tired-she is exhausted from the constant scanning, the bracing for something bad to happen.

Her sleep is broken. She dreams of headlights and shouting voices. She wakes up with her jaw clenched and her hands curled into fists. She has stopped attending community events because the sight of a uniform-any uniform-makes her stomach drop. Last month, a student's parent, a police officer, came to pick up their child during dismissal. A. saw him at the front desk and immediately walked the other way, leaving a colleague to handle the sign-out. She felt ashamed, but the shame only deepened the numbness that has settled over her like a fog.

She recently told Kofi the full story, crying for the first time in a year. He held her and said nothing, which she needed. But the relief was brief. The next day, at work, a seventh-grader mentioned her uncle was a cop. A. felt her chest tighten. She smiled and changed the subject.

A. still goes to work every day. She still helps children. But she is no longer the same person who sat in that car on the side of the road. She moves through her life in a state of quiet vigilance, waiting for another moment that will confirm what she has already learned: that safety is an illusion, and that some stories cannot be talked away.
